t: Vulva and vagina: infections and lesions
sub: How pH and a wet mount separate the three causes of vaginitis, and which vulvar and vaginal lesions lead to cancer.

pretest.q: A vaginal discharge has a pH of 5.0, a fishy odor after adding KOH, and epithelial cells coated with bacteria. Which organism has overgrown?
pretest.why: Bacterial vaginosis replaces lactobacilli with Gardnerella and other anaerobes. Their amines give the fishy whiff, the lost lactic acid raises the pH, and bacteria coating squamous cells make clue cells.

w.Candida albicans: Candida leaves the pH normal and shows budding yeast with pseudohyphae on a KOH prep, not bacteria-coated clue cells.
w.Trichomonas vaginalis: Trichomonads also raise the pH, but the wet mount shows motile flagellated protozoa rather than clue cells, and the discharge is frothy.
w.Lactobacillus crispatus: Lactobacilli are the protective flora that keep the pH at 3.8 to 4.5; their loss, not their overgrowth, causes vaginosis.

pretest.q: An older woman with lichen sclerosus has a vulvar precursor lesion. Which staining pattern is expected?
o: Aberrant p53 with absent or patchy p16
Diffuse block p16 with wild-type p53
pretest.why: Lichen sclerosus leads to differentiated VIN, an HPV-independent lesion driven by TP53 mutation. The mutant p53 stains aberrantly, and without HPV E7 there is no p16 overexpression.

w.Diffuse block p16 with wild-type p53: Block p16 marks high-risk HPV acting through E7, the pattern of HSIL in younger women, not the lichen sclerosus pathway.
w.S100 and HMB-45 positive cells: These markers identify melanocytic lesions such as melanoma; squamous precursors and Paget cells are negative for them.
w.Desmin and myogenin positive cells: Muscle markers identify rhabdomyosarcoma, such as sarcoma botryoides in young girls, not a squamous precursor.

pretest.q: A 27-year-old has severe unilateral vulvar pain and a tender, fluctuant mass at the posterolateral vestibule. Which structure is obstructed?
o: Sebaceous gland of the labium majus
pretest.why: Bartholin glands lie at the posterolateral introitus, at about 4 and 8 o'clock. A blocked duct traps mucus as a cyst, and infection makes the painful, fluctuant abscess seen here, treated by drainage with a Word catheter or marsupialization.

w.Skene gland duct: Skene (paraurethral) glands open beside the urethra, so their infection causes dysuria or urethral discharge rather than a vestibular mass.
w.Gartner duct remnant: A Gartner duct cyst is a mesonephric remnant on the lateral vaginal wall, usually painless and not at the introitus, so it does not form this abscess.
w.Sebaceous gland of the labium majus: A sebaceous cyst lies in the skin of the labium majus and is usually small and painless; the vestibular site and fluctuant abscess point to the Bartholin duct.

body: What keeps a healthy vagina acidic and moist?

The vagina is lined by **nonkeratinized stratified squamous epithelium**, a surface that resists friction but has no glands of its own. Under estrogen its cells fill with **glycogen**, and resident **lactobacilli** ferment that glycogen into lactic acid, so the normal pH sits between 3.8 and 4.5. Because the acid keeps most pathogens from growing, anything that removes lactobacilli or estrogen raises the pH and invites infection. That is why girls before puberty and women after menopause, who store little glycogen, have a higher vaginal pH.

The wall is built for distensibility, not for secretion. Beneath the epithelium, a lamina propria rich in **elastic** fibers and a dense venous plexus covers smooth muscle, and the mucosa is thrown into transverse folds, the **rugae**, that flatten as the canal distends in childbirth. During arousal, congestion of the venous plexus forces plasma through the epithelium as a **transudate**, and this fluid mixes with cervical and vestibular mucus to lubricate the canal. After menopause low estrogen thins the epithelium and flattens the rugae, so atrophic vaginitis brings dryness, burning and painful intercourse.
pH is the first branch point

A vaginal pH **above 4.5** means the lactobacillus barrier has failed, which happens in bacterial vaginosis and trichomoniasis. A normal pH with itching and discharge points to **candidiasis**, because Candida can overgrow even while lactobacilli keep the vagina acidic.
Which glands lubricate the vestibule, and what happens when a duct blocks?

The paired {{rp12_bartholin|Bartholin glands}}, or greater vestibular glands, lie deep in the posterior vestibule and drain by ducts that open at about 4 and 8 o'clock. Their mucus-secreting acini make mucin, and the duct is lined by **transitional epithelium**, so the glands lubricate the introitus, above all during arousal. When a duct blocks, mucus collects as a cyst; infection, usually polymicrobial, turns it into a painful, fluctuant abscess in the posterolateral vestibule. Treatment keeps a drainage tract open, either with a **Word catheter**, a small inflatable balloon left in place for several weeks, or by **marsupialization**, which sews the cyst wall open. A persistent mass in a woman over 40 is biopsied, because Bartholin gland carcinoma, though rare, looks the same.

The smaller **paraurethral (Skene) glands**, the female counterpart of the prostate, open beside the urethral meatus and keep it moist, so their infections cause urethral symptoms such as dysuria rather than a vestibular mass. A **Gartner duct cyst** is different again: it sits on the lateral vaginal wall, because it is a leftover piece of the mesonephric duct.
How do you tell the three common causes of vaginitis apart?

**Bacterial vaginosis** is the most common cause of abnormal discharge in women of reproductive age. It is a shift in the flora rather than an invasion: lactobacilli fall and **Gardnerella vaginalis** and other anaerobes overgrow. Anaerobes make amines, so the thin, gray, homogeneous discharge smells fishy, and adding potassium hydroxide releases a stronger odor, the **whiff test**. On a saline wet mount, {{rp12_clue|clue cells}} appear, and white cells are scarce because the process is not inflammatory. Amsel criteria make the diagnosis when three of four are present: typical discharge, pH above 4.5, a positive whiff test and clue cells.

Vaginosis is treated with **metronidazole**, a 7-day oral course, or clindamycin because it raises the risk of pelvic inflammatory disease and, in pregnancy, of preterm birth and premature rupture of membranes. Symptomatic pregnant women are treated, but women without symptoms are not screened. Metronidazole is a prodrug: anaerobes and protozoa reduce its nitro group into radicals that break their DNA, so one drug covers vaginosis and trichomoniasis. Step 1 references still list a disulfiram-like reaction with alcohol, but the 2021 CDC guidelines found no convincing evidence for it and no longer tell patients to avoid alcohol.

**Trichomoniasis** is a sexually transmitted infection by *Trichomonas vaginalis*, a pear-shaped, **flagellated** protozoan. It causes a profuse, frothy, yellow-green discharge and a pH above 4.5, and punctate hemorrhages on the cervix give the classic **strawberry cervix**. A wet mount shows motile trichomonads but misses many infections, so nucleic acid amplification testing is more sensitive. The patient takes a 7-day course of metronidazole, every recent partner is treated, and she is retested within three months because reinfection is common. The infection raises the risk of acquiring HIV and, in pregnancy, of preterm birth, so symptomatic pregnant women are treated too.

**Vulvovaginal candidiasis** is overgrowth of *Candida albicans* when the host balance shifts: antibiotics that kill lactobacilli, diabetes or SGLT2 inhibitors that put sugar in the urine, pregnancy, or immunosuppression. The discharge is thick, white and curdlike, itching dominates, and the pH stays normal. A potassium hydroxide prep dissolves the squamous cells and leaves budding yeast and **pseudohyphae** in view. A single oral dose of **fluconazole**, which blocks fungal ergosterol synthesis, cures most episodes; topical azoles are used in pregnancy, and partners are not treated. Three or more episodes in a year need a longer induction course and weekly maintenance fluconazole, and species that resist fluconazole, such as *Candida glabrata*, are treated with vaginal boric acid.
Thin, gray, fishy; positive whiff test
Partners are treated for trichomoniasis, not for yeast

Trichomoniasis is sexually transmitted, so every recent partner gets metronidazole, and an untreated partner reinfects her. Candidiasis is not sexually transmitted, so partners are not treated. Giving an antibiotic for a yeast infection makes it worse, because the antibiotic kills the lactobacilli that were holding Candida back.
Working up vaginal discharge at the bedside
Touch pH paper to the lateral vaginal wall; a value above 4.5 points toward bacterial vaginosis or trichomoniasis, while a normal value favors candidiasis.
Add potassium hydroxide to the discharge; a fishy amine odor supports bacterial vaginosis because the overgrowing anaerobes produce those amines.
Clue cells mean bacterial vaginosis, and motile flagellated trichomonads swimming across the field mean trichomoniasis.
Potassium hydroxide dissolves squamous cells so that budding yeast and pseudohyphae stand out, confirming candidiasis.
Send a NAAT when microscopy is negative
Nucleic acid amplification catches trichomoniasis that a wet mount missed and tests for gonorrhea and chlamydia at the same visit.
How does cervicitis differ from vaginitis?

Vaginitis inflames the vaginal wall and changes the discharge; {{rp12_cervicitis|cervicitis}} inflames the cervix and shows at the os. The usual causes are infectious: *Chlamydia trachomatis*, the most common, and *Neisseria gonorrhoeae*, followed by trichomonads and herpes simplex virus, with bacterial vaginosis a frequent companion. Douches, spermicides and tampons are noninfectious irritants. Many women have no symptoms; others have **mucopurulent** discharge from the os, bleeding after intercourse and a friable cervix that bleeds when the swab touches it. Trichomonads leave punctate hemorrhages, the strawberry cervix, and herpes leaves ulcers.

A nucleic acid amplification test on a vaginal swab or urine detects chlamydia, gonorrhea and trichomonas, and a pH and wet mount check for vaginitis at the same visit, because the two often coexist. Women at high risk are treated at once with doxycycline, and ceftriaxone is added when gonorrhea is likely; partners are treated and the patient is retested after about 3 months. Untreated infection ascends to cause pelvic inflammatory disease, infertility and ectopic pregnancy.
Which white vulvar lesions carry a cancer risk?

{{rp12_lsa|Lichen sclerosus}} is a chronic, T-cell-mediated dermatosis, often seen with other autoimmune disease, that affects postmenopausal women and prepubertal girls. The skin turns thin, white and wrinkled like parchment in a **figure-of-eight** around the vulva and anus, and the vagina is spared. Biopsy shows a thin epidermis without rete ridges; beneath it the collagen is homogenized, the **dermal sclerosis** that names the disease, with a band of lymphocytes below. Itching and scarring follow, and the introitus can narrow. An ultrapotent **topical corticosteroid** such as clobetasol controls it. The lesion is not itself premalignant, but it carries a small risk of squamous cell carcinoma, so a new ulcer or thick plaque is biopsied.

**Lichen simplex chronicus**, which pathologists also call squamous cell hyperplasia, is the opposite picture. An itch-scratch cycle thickens the skin into a leathery white plaque. Biopsy shows acanthosis, hyperkeratosis and elongated rete ridges without atypia, and there is no cancer risk; steroids and stopping the scratching break the cycle. Because the two white plaques look alike, a persistent one is biopsied to exclude vulvar intraepithelial neoplasia. **Lichen planus** is also T-cell mediated but erosive: raw red vestibular patches with lacy white borders that extend into the vagina and often the mouth, where scarring can narrow the vaginal canal.
What else causes vulvar itching, burning or dryness?

Not every sore or itchy vulva is infection or neoplasia. **Contact dermatitis** follows an irritant such as antiseptic wipes, pads, soaps or urine, or less often an allergen, and shows as a sharply bordered red, weeping patch within days. **Vulvodynia** is vulvar pain lasting at least three months with no identifiable cause, and it is a common cause of painful intercourse before menopause. Both are diagnosed from the history and exam after infection and dermatoses are excluded.
Itch or burning after a new product, with sharply bordered redness; history, and patch testing if allergy is suspected
Remove the trigger; bland emollients; short course of topical steroid
Burning pain on touch or penetration with normal skin; cotton-swab test after infection and dermatoses are excluded
Pelvic floor physical therapy, neuropathic pain agents, cognitive behavioral therapy
Dry, pale, thin mucosa, lost rugae and pH above 4.5; exam to rule out infection
How do HPV-driven and HPV-independent vulvar cancers differ?

Low-risk HPV types 6 and 11 cause **condyloma acuminatum**, soft cauliflower-like warts whose squamous cells are koilocytes, with a clear halo around a wrinkled, dark nucleus. Condylomas signal HPV exposure but do not become cancer. High-risk HPV, mainly type 16, causes a high-grade squamous intraepithelial lesion, the usual type of **vulvar intraepithelial neoplasia** (VIN), in younger women who often smoke or are immunosuppressed. Its E7 protein inactivates Rb, which drives strong, diffuse block staining for **p16**, while p53 stains in a normal, wild-type pattern. These lesions progress to warty or basaloid squamous carcinoma.

The other road starts in lichen sclerosus. In older women a **TP53 mutation** produces {{rp12_dvin|differentiated VIN}}, in which only the basal cells look atypical while the surface still matures, so it is easy to underdiagnose. It stains aberrantly for p53 and is negative or patchy for p16 because HPV plays no part. This road leads to keratinizing squamous cell carcinoma, the more common type of **vulvar carcinoma**. Whichever road it takes, vulvar carcinoma spreads first to the **superficial inguinal lymph nodes**.
p16 marks HPV; p53 marks the other road

Diffuse block **p16** staining is a surrogate for active high-risk HPV and points to HSIL and warty or basaloid carcinoma. **Aberrant p53** with absent or patchy p16 points to differentiated VIN, lichen sclerosus and keratinizing carcinoma in an older woman.
Why does p16 stain so strongly in HPV-driven lesions when p16 normally stops the cell cycle?

p16 is a brake that works through Rb: it inhibits the cyclin D and CDK4/6 complex that would phosphorylate and inactivate Rb. When Rb is working, it keeps p16 production low through feedback. High-risk HPV E7 binds and disables Rb directly, so E2F is released and the cell keeps dividing. Losing Rb activity removes the feedback, and the cell makes large amounts of p16. Because p16 acts upstream of Rb, the extra brake cannot stop a cycle that E7 has already switched on. Diffuse block staining for p16 therefore marks transcriptionally active high-risk HPV.

{{rp12_emp|Extramammary Paget disease}} is the vulvar plaque that fools clinicians: a red, scaly, eczema-like patch that itches and does not improve with topical steroids. It is an **intraepithelial adenocarcinoma**: biopsy shows large, pale **Paget cells** scattered singly and in clusters through the epidermis. Their mucin is PAS-positive and they stain for keratin (CK7) and CEA but not for S100 or HMB-45, which excludes melanoma. Unlike Paget disease of the nipple, which almost always sits on a breast carcinoma, vulvar Paget disease usually has no underlying carcinoma. Wide local excision is the treatment, and it often recurs because the cells spread beyond the visible edge.

Any persistent, ulcerated, pigmented or treatment-resistant lesion is biopsied, because the surface cannot separate a dermatosis from a neoplasm. HSIL is excised, or treated with imiquimod or laser when it is multifocal. Invasive vulvar carcinoma needs **wide local excision** with a margin of normal skin, and when invasion exceeds 1 mm the groin nodes are assessed by sentinel node biopsy or inguinofemoral lymphadenectomy. Node status is the strongest prognostic factor, and radiation treats positive nodes or large tumors.
Which vaginal tumors depend on age and exposure?

Primary vaginal squamous carcinoma is rare and HPV-related, and most squamous carcinoma found in the vagina has spread from the cervix. Radiation is its main treatment, because surgery would sacrifice the bladder or rectum. Young women whose mothers took **diethylstilbestrol (DES)**, a synthetic estrogen once given to prevent miscarriage, can develop **vaginal adenosis**, glandular paramesonephric (Müllerian) epithelium that persists in the upper vagina, and rarely **clear cell adenocarcinoma**, with glycogen-filled clear cells and hobnail nuclei. In girls younger than 5, {{rp12_botry|sarcoma botryoides}}, the botryoid form of embryonal rhabdomyosarcoma, pushes a grape-like, bleeding polypoid mass out of the vagina.

Under the microscope, sarcoma botryoides shows **small round blue cells** crowded into a dense **cambium layer** just beneath the intact epithelium. Some tumor cells are rhabdomyoblasts with pink cytoplasm and cross-striations, and the cells stain for the muscle proteins **desmin**, myogenin and MyoD1, which separates the tumor from other small round blue cell tumors. Chemotherapy with limited surgery cures most children.
Young woman exposed to DES in utero

body.q: A patient has itching, thick white discharge and a vaginal pH of 4.2. Which reasoning best narrows the cause?
o: A normal pH means the lactobacilli are intact, which fits Candida, an organism that can overgrow in an acidic vagina
A normal pH rules out infection, so the symptoms must come from an irritant or an allergy
Itching with discharge means trichomoniasis until proven otherwise, because trichomonads thrive in an acidic vagina
A pH of 4.2 means anaerobes have replaced the lactobacilli, which defines bacterial vaginosis
body.why: Bacterial vaginosis and trichomoniasis both raise the pH above 4.5, the first because lactobacilli are lost and the second because the protozoan disrupts the flora. Candida is different: it tolerates an acidic vagina and can overgrow while lactobacilli still hold the pH at 3.8 to 4.5. A normal pH therefore does not rule out infection; it sends you to a KOH prep to look for budding yeast and pseudohyphae.

grid.q: Which of these findings fit bacterial vaginosis?
items: Clue cells on a saline wet mount
Fishy odor after adding potassium hydroxide
Few white cells on the wet mount
Normal vaginal pH with intense itching
